claim: Mdn1 is an essential AAA mechanoenzyme that drives at least two separate steps in ribosome biogenesis.
source: The essential AAA (ATPase associated with diverse cellular activities) mechanoenzyme Mdn1 drives at least two separate steps in ribosome biogenesis, using its MIDAS domain to extract the ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain-containing proteins Rsa4 and Ytm1 from ribosomal precursors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior work throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mdn1 uses its MIDAS domain to extract the UBL domain-containing proteins Rsa4 and Ytm1 from ribosomal precursors.
source: The essential AAA (ATPase associated with diverse cellular activities) mechanoenzyme Mdn1 drives at least two separate steps in ribosome biogenesis, using its MIDAS domain to extract the ubiquitin-like (UBL) domain-containing proteins Rsa4 and Ytm1 from ribosomal precursors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies (Bassler et al., 2010; Ulbrich et al., 2009).

claim: Forces up to ~4 pN enhance the MIDAS domain binding lifetime to Rsa4 and Ytm1 up to 10-fold.
source: Parallel experiments with Rsa4 and Ytm1 show that forces up to ~4 pN, matching the magnitude of force produced by AAA proteins similar to Mdn1, enhance the MIDAS domain binding lifetime up to 10-fold, and higher forces accelerate dissociation.
evidence: This is directly measured in the optical tweezers experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Higher forces (above ~4 pN) accelerate dissociation of the MIDAS-UBL interaction.
source: Parallel experiments with Rsa4 and Ytm1 show that forces up to ~4 pN, matching the magnitude of force produced by AAA proteins similar to Mdn1, enhance the MIDAS domain binding lifetime up to 10-fold, and higher forces accelerate dissociation.
evidence: This is directly measured in the optical tweezers experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Mdn1's MIDAS domain can form catch bonds with more than one UBL substrate.
source: Together, our studies indicate that Mdn1's MIDAS domain can form catch bonds with more than one UBL substrate, and provide insights into how mechanoregulation may contribute to the Mdn1 enzymatic cycle during ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the optical tweezers experiments with both Rsa4 and Ytm1 showing catch bond behavior.

claim: Catch bonds are a form of mechanoregulation wherein protein-ligand interactions are strengthened by the application of dissociative tension.
source: Catch bonds are a form of mechanoregulation wherein protein-ligand interactions are strengthened by the application of dissociative tension.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the abstract and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Most protein-ligand interactions become weaker when external forces are applied along the bond axis (slip bonds).
source: While most protein-ligand interactions are known to become weaker when external forces are applied along the bond axis, referred to as slip bonds, a few special cases have been identified where force increases bond lifetimes, referred to as catch bonds (Bell, 1978; Sokurenko et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to foundational work on bond mechanics.

claim: Catch bonds are hypothesized to be a widely used regulatory mechanism in the cell.
source: Catch bonds are hypothesized to be a widely used regulatory mechanism in the cell (Sokurenko et al., 2008), but force spectroscopy investigations to date have largely focused on cell adhesion and cytoskeleton proteins.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to Sokurenko et al., 2008.

claim: Most known examples of catch bonds are for one protein interacting with one specific substrate.
source: Moreover, most known examples of catch bonds are for one protein interacting with one specific substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as context for the novelty of the current findings.

claim: Mdn1 is a large (>500 kDa) multi-domain enzyme.
source: Mdn1 is a large (>500 kDa) multi-domain enzyme; at its N-terminus are six AAA domains, which fold into a pseudohexameric ring, followed by a linker including both a structured (~1800 amino acids) and a likely non-structured (~517 amino acids) region, and finally a C-terminal (290 amino acid) MIDAS domain (Figure 1A; Garbarino and Gibbons, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to Figure 1A and citation to Garbarino and Gibbons, 2002.

claim: Mdn1 has six AAA domains at its N-terminus that fold into a pseudohexameric ring.
source: Mdn1 is a large (>500 kDa) multi-domain enzyme; at its N-terminus are six AAA domains, which fold into a pseudohexameric ring, followed by a linker including both a structured (~1800 amino acids) and a likely non-structured (~517 amino acids) region, and finally a C-terminal (290 amino acid) MIDAS domain (Figure 1A; Garbarino and Gibbons, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with reference to Figure 1A and citation to Garbarino and Gibbons, 2002.

claim: The Mdn1 MIDAS domain bears structural homology to the integrin α I domain.
source: The Mdn1 MIDAS domain bears structural homology to the integrin α I domain (Garbarino and Gibbons, 2002).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Garbarino and Gibbons, 2002.

claim: The integrin α I domain has a weak (~1 mM) affinity for its ligands in solution.
source: In solution, this integrin domain has a weak (~1 mM) affinity for its ligands (Shimaoka et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Shimaoka et al., 2001.

claim: The integrin α I domain affinity can be enhanced by about an order of magnitude by applied force.
source: Remarkably, this affinity can be enhanced by about an order of magnitude by applied force (Astrof et al., 2006; Kong et al., 2009; Shimaoka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citations to studies on integrin mechanobiology.

claim: Brownian dynamics simulations show that docking of the MIDAS domain onto the AAA ring stretches the unstructured portion of the linker such that 1–2 pN of tension is generated.
source: Consistent with this idea, Brownian dynamics simulations have shown that docking of the MIDAS domain onto the AAA ring stretches the unstructured portion of the linker such that 1–2 pN of tension is generated (Mickolajczyk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation to a previous computational study by the authors.

claim: Rsa4-GFP was confirmed to be a monomer of the correct molecular weight by native mass spectrometry (to within 20 Da).
source: Rsa4-GFP was confirmed to be a monomer of the correct molecular weight both by native mass spectrometry (nMS) (to within 20 Da; Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and by mass photometry (to within 2 kDa; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1D and supplementary figures showing the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Rsa4-GFP was confirmed to be a monomer of the correct molecular weight by mass photometry (to within 2 kDa).
source: Rsa4-GFP was confirmed to be a monomer of the correct molecular weight both by native mass spectrometry (nMS) (to within 20 Da; Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and by mass photometry (to within 2 kDa; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary figure showing the mass photometry data.

claim: Mixing Rsa4 with MIDAS-WT before injection led to a shift in the fluorescence profile toward a higher molecular weight, consistent with binding.
source: Mixing Rsa4 with MIDAS-WT before injection led to a shift in the fluorescence profile toward a higher molecular weight, with an overlapping elution profile consistent with binding (Figure 1E–F, blue).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1E-F showing the size exclusion chromatography data.

claim: Mixing Rsa4 with MIDAS-Y6664R before injection did not lead to a shift in the fluorescence profile or to apparent coelution by SDS-PAGE.
source: Mixing Rsa4 with MIDAS-Y6664R before injection did not lead to a shift in the fluorescence profile or to apparent coelution by SDS-PAGE (Figure 1E–F, red), suggesting that the coelution with MIDAS-WT is due to specific binding.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1E-F showing the size exclusion chromatography data.

claim: The Mdn1 MIDAS domain has a KD of 6.9 ± 2.0 μM for Rsa4-GFP as measured by microscale thermophoresis.
source: Titrating MIDAS-WT against Rsa4-GFP (50 nM) produced changes in the normalized fluorescence signal upon heating (|ΔFNorm|) that could be fitted to a binding isotherm with KD = 6.9 ± 2.0 μM (fit ±95% confidence intervals, CI) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1G showing the MST data and fitted binding curve.

claim: The Mdn1 MIDAS domain has weak affinity (~7 μM) for Rsa4 in solution.
source: Together, these results show that while the Mdn1 MIDAS domain can bind to Rsa4 in solution, the binding affinity is weak (~7 μM).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the MST experiments.

claim: The distribution of bond lifetimes for MIDAS-WT with Rsa4 at 6 pN could be fitted to a single exponential.
source: The distribution (n = 57 events from 14 molecules) of bond lifetimes could be fitted to a single exponential (appears linear on a semilog plot) as opposed to a higher-order exponential (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), consistent with the kinetics of exit from a single bound state (Guo and Guilford, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary figure showing the fitting analysis.

claim: MIDAS-Y4666R has a substantially shorter bond lifetime with Rsa4-GFP versus MIDAS-WT, providing evidence that the binding events measured are specific.
source: The substantially shorter bond lifetime distribution of MIDAS-Y4666R with Rsa4-GFP versus MIDAS-WT provides evidence that the binding events measured are specific.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of bond lifetime distributions shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The average bond lifetime increased between FTot values of 4–8 pN, and then decreased at FTot values of 10–12 pN.
source: The average bond lifetime increased between FTot values of 4–8 pN, and then decreased at FTot values of 10–12 pN.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The stabilization of binding by external load up to a certain threshold (catch bond) contrasts the more common scenario where external force monotonically accelerates dissociation (slip bond).
source: This stabilization of binding by external load up to a certain threshold (catch bond) contrasts the more common scenario where external force monotonically accelerates dissociation (slip bond).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the force-dependent bond lifetime data.

claim: The inextensible length of the proteins (Lprot) is estimated to be 8 nm based on existing structural data.
source: where Lprot is the inextensible length of the proteins. Based on existing structural data, we estimate Lprot to be 8 nm (Ahmed et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section with citation to structural data.

claim: The critical force at which bond lifetime is maximized for MIDAS-Rsa4 is estimated to be 4.2 pN.
source: Additionally, this fit allowed us to determine the critical force at which bond lifetime is maximized, which we estimated to be 4.2 pN.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on fitting the catch-slip Bell model to the data.

claim: The Mdn1 MIDAS domain forms a catch bond with Rsa4.
source: Overall, this analysis shows that the Mdn1 MIDAS domain forms a catch bond with Rsa4.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the optical tweezers experiments and analysis.

claim: The Schizosaccharomyces pombe Rsa4 and Ytm1 UBL domains only have 43.0% sequence similarity.
source: However, the Schizosaccharomyces pombe Rsa4 and Ytm1 UBL domains only have 43.0% sequence similarity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as context for testing whether catch bond behavior is general.

claim: Ytm1-GFP was assessed to be homogenous, monomeric, and centered around the expected molecular weight by both native mass spectrometry (to within 20 Da) and mass photometry (to within 1 kDa).
source: Ytm1-GFP ran with an apparent double-banding pattern (Figure 4A), however the protein was assessed to be homogenous, monomeric, and centered around the expected molecular weight by both nMS (to within 20 Da) and mass photometry (to within 1 kDa; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary figure showing the characterization data.

claim: Coelution was seen for Ytm1-GFP with MIDAS-WT but not with MIDAS-Y4666R.
source: We ran size exclusion chromatography assays, and as with Rsa4-GFP, coelution was seen for Ytm1-GFP with MIDAS-WT but not with MIDAS-Y4666R (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4B-C showing the size exclusion chromatography data.

claim: MIDAS and Ytm1-GFP can bind in solution, but interaction is even weaker than that of MIDAS and Rsa4-GFP.
source: Hence. MIDAS and Ytm1-GFP can bind in solution, but interaction is even weaker than that of MIDAS and Rsa4-GFP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on MST data that could not be fitted to a binding isotherm.

claim: Mdn1 MIDAS can form a catch bond with Ytm1-GFP.
source: Plotting the average bond lifetime as a function of FLoad, the force experienced by the proteins in the force jump assay, we found that Mdn1 MIDAS can form a catch bond with Ytm1-GFP (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 4F showing the force-dependent bond lifetime data.

claim: The critical force where binding lifetime is maximized for MIDAS-Ytm1 was 3.3 pN, versus 4.2 pN for Rsa4-GFP.
source: The critical force where binding lifetime is maximized was 3.3 pN, versus 4.2 pN for Rsa4-GFP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on fitting the catch-slip Bell model to the Ytm1 data.

claim: The Mdn1 MIDAS domain forms a catch bond with two different UBL domain-containing proteins.
source: Overall, these results show that the Mdn1 MIDAS domain forms a catch bond with two different UBL domain-containing proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the optical tweezers experiments with both Rsa4 and Ytm1.

claim: The Mdn1 MIDAS domain has weak affinity for Rsa4 and Ytm1 in solution (≥7 μM).
source: We show that the Mdn1 MIDAS domain has weak affinity for Rsa4 and Ytm1 in solution (≥7 μM).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the bulk binding measurements.

claim: Mdn1 MIDAS forms a catch bond with both Rsa4 and Ytm1, with bond lifetimes increasing by an order of magnitude under applied tension up to ~4 pN.
source: Using a single-molecule optical tweezers force jump assay developed for this study, we show that Mdn1 MIDAS forms a catch bond with both Rsa4 and Ytm1, with bond lifetimes increasing by an order of magnitude under applied tension up to ~4 pN, and decreasing back to baseline between ~4 and 10 pN.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the optical tweezers measurements.

claim: Bond lifetimes decrease back to baseline between ~4 and 10 pN for MIDAS-Rsa4 and MIDAS-Ytm1 interactions.
source: Using a single-molecule optical tweezers force jump assay developed for this study, we show that Mdn1 MIDAS forms a catch bond with both Rsa4 and Ytm1, with bond lifetimes increasing by an order of magnitude under applied tension up to ~4 pN, and decreasing back to baseline between ~4 and 10 pN.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section summarizing the optical tweezers measurements.

claim: Mdn1 binds the pre-60S particle and establishes a tripartite interaction between its AAA ring, its MIDAS domain, and the UBL domain of the assembly factor substrate.
source: Mdn1 binds the pre-60S particle and establishes a tripartite interaction between its AAA ring, its MIDAS domain, and the UBL domain of the assembly factor substrate that it must extract (Chen et al., 2018; Kater et al., 2020; Sosnowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to structural studies.

claim: In the MIDAS-docked state, Mdn1's unstructured linker is stretched and acts as an entropic spring.
source: In this MIDAS-docked state, Mdn1's unstructured linker, which acts as an entropic spring, is stretched; computational modeling of MIDAS docking estimates that 1–2 pN of tension is built up and propagated along the MIDAS-UBL bond axis (Mickolajczyk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to a previous computational study.

claim: Computational modeling of MIDAS docking estimates that 1–2 pN of tension is built up and propagated along the MIDAS-UBL bond axis.
source: In this MIDAS-docked state, Mdn1's unstructured linker, which acts as an entropic spring, is stretched; computational modeling of MIDAS docking estimates that 1–2 pN of tension is built up and propagated along the MIDAS-UBL bond axis (Mickolajczyk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to a previous computational study.

claim: A catch bond mechanism helps to explain how tension promotes, rather than disfavors, MIDAS-UBL binding.
source: A catch bond mechanism helps to explain how this tension promotes, rather than disfavors, MIDAS-UBL binding; 1–2 pN is below the ~3.3–4.2 pN peak of the MIDAS-UBL catch bond, but one possibility is that additional tension is generated by Mdn1's ATPase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the catch bond findings.

claim: Additional tension may be generated by Mdn1's ATPase activity.
source: A catch bond mechanism helps to explain how this tension promotes, rather than disfavors, MIDAS-UBL binding; 1–2 pN is below the ~3.3–4.2 pN peak of the MIDAS-UBL catch bond, but one possibility is that additional tension is generated by Mdn1's ATPase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculative possibility.

claim: Ytm1 and Rsa4 removal occur at separate stages of pre-60S maturation, in the nucleolus and nucleoplasm, respectively.
source: Ytm1 and Rsa4 removal occur at separate stages of pre-60S maturation, in the nucleolus and nucleoplasm, respectively (Bassler et al., 2010; Kressler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to studies on ribosome biogenesis.

claim: Free copies of Ytm1 and Rsa4 are present in the nucleolus and nucleoplasm.
source: We also note that free copies of Ytm1 and Rsa4 are present in the nucleolus and nucleoplasm (Kressler et al., 2012); the Mdn1 catch bond thus also prevents Mdn1-Rsa4/Ytm1 binding while off the pre-60S, which would compete away usable copies of each protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Kressler et al., 2012.

claim: The Mdn1 catch bond prevents Mdn1-Rsa4/Ytm1 binding while off the pre-60S, which would compete away usable copies of each protein.
source: We also note that free copies of Ytm1 and Rsa4 are present in the nucleolus and nucleoplasm (Kressler et al., 2012); the Mdn1 catch bond thus also prevents Mdn1-Rsa4/Ytm1 binding while off the pre-60S, which would compete away usable copies of each protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the catch bond mechanism.

claim: The UBL domains of Rsa4 and Ytm1 have low sequence similarity (43.0% in S. pombe), but a high level of structural similarity.
source: The UBL domains of Rsa4 and Ytm1 have low sequence similarity (43.0% in S. pombe), but a high level of structural similarity (Ahmed et al., 2019; Romes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to structural studies.

claim: There are numerous (>10 in S. pombe, >60 in humans) other UBL domain-containing proteins with similar folds to Ytm1/Rsa4-UBL.
source: There are numerous (>10 in S. pombe, >60 in humans) other UBL domain-containing proteins with similar folds to Ytm1/Rsa4-UBL (Collins and Goldberg, 2020; Hartmann-Petersen and Gordon, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to reviews on UBL domains.

claim: Mdn1 in mammalian cells has been shown to be targeted to SUMOylated substrates.
source: In addition, Mdn1 in mammalian cells has been shown to be targeted to SUMOylated substrates (Raman et al., 2016), where SUMO and UBL domains also share structural similarity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Raman et al., 2016.

claim: Mdn1 was recently implicated to also have a role in heterochromatic RNA clearance.
source: While no Mdn1 MIDAS-binding partners other than Rsa4 and Ytm1 have been confirmed to date, it is noteworthy that Mdn1 was recently implicated to also have a role in heterochromatic RNA clearance (Shipkovenska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Shipkovenska et al., 2020.

claim: Mdn1 may process UBL or SUMO domain-containing proteins other than Rsa4 and Ytm1 in the cell.
source: Therefore, we speculate that Mdn1 may also process UBL or SUMO domain-containing proteins other than Rsa4 and Ytm1 in the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on the structural similarity of UBL domains and the catch bond findings.

claim: The Mdn1 MIDAS domain would form catch bonds with putative UBL or SUMO domain-containing substrates other than Rsa4 and Ytm1.
source: Based on the close similarity of the Rsa4 and Ytm1 catch bonds measured, we predict that the Mdn1 MIDAS domain would also form catch bonds with these putative substrates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a prediction based on the similarity of the Rsa4 and Ytm1 catch bonds.

claim: Integrin has been shown to form catch bonds with a fragment of its substrate containing the RGD consensus sequence.
source: Integrin has also been shown to form catch bonds, albeit with a fragment of its substrate (containing the RGD consensus sequence) rather than with two different full-length, folded proteins (Astrof et al., 2006; Kong et al., 2009; Puklin-Faucher et al., 2006; Shimaoka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to studies on integrin catch bonds.

claim: The critical force at which bond lifetime is maximized is ~10–30 pN for integrin.
source: Interestingly, the critical force at which bond lifetime is maximized is ~10–30 pN for integrin (Chen et al., 2011; Kong et al., 2009), a force-range relevant for meso-scale cell adhesions, in contrast to ~4 pN for Mdn1 MIDAS (Figures 3G and 4F), matching the forces that dynein, a AAA protein with high sequence similarity to Mdn1, is capable of producing (4.3 pN) (Belyy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to studies on integrin and dynein mechanics.

claim: Dynein, a AAA protein with high sequence similarity to Mdn1, is capable of producing 4.3 pN of force.
source: Interestingly, the critical force at which bond lifetime is maximized is ~10–30 pN for integrin (Chen et al., 2011; Kong et al., 2009), a force-range relevant for meso-scale cell adhesions, in contrast to ~4 pN for Mdn1 MIDAS (Figures 3G and 4F), matching the forces that dynein, a AAA protein with high sequence similarity to Mdn1, is capable of producing (4.3 pN) (Belyy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Belyy et al., 2016.

claim: MIDAS domains can be tuned to form catch bonds at forces ranging from the single motor to the multi-motor regime, as needed for specific cellular contexts.
source: We therefore suggest that MIDAS domains can be tuned to form catch bonds at forces ranging from the single motor to the multi-motor regime, as needed for specific cellular contexts.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from comparing the critical forces for Mdn1 MIDAS and integrin.

claim: Numerous AAA motor proteins including CbbQ, Vwa8, magnesium chelatase, and others either contain or couple their activities with MIDAS domains.
source: Toward this end, numerous AAA motor proteins including CbbQ (Sutter et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2015; Tsai et al., 2020), Vwa8 (Luo et al., 2017), magnesium chelatase (Fodje et al., 2001), and others (Iyer et al., 2004), as well as other proteins with known mechanical activation such as von Willebrand factor (Fredrickson et al., 1998; Kim et al., 2010; Ruggeri and Ware, 1993), either contain or couple their activities with MIDAS domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to studies on various MIDAS-containing proteins.

claim: The force jump assay applies force at a very high rate (~20,000 pN/s).
source: Similar to other experimental geometries used to measure catch bonds (Guo and Guilford, 2006; Huang et al., 2017), our force jump assay applies force at a very high rate (~20,000 pN/s), which may influence protein-protein binding (Rao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of the force jump assay.

claim: The shortest binding durations measured (20 ms) are >100-fold longer than the estimated rise time of the force jump.
source: Nonetheless, we note that we use the same assay for all proteins in this study, and that the shortest binding durations we measure (20 ms) are >100-fold longer than the estimated rise time of the force jump.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section to address the potential concern about the high force loading rate.

claim: Catch bonds are an example of how mechanical forces can directly regulate essential protein-ligand interactions.
source: Catch bonds are an example of how mechanical forces can directly regulate essential protein-ligand interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a general principle.

claim: Mechanoregulation is nearly instantaneous and reversible without the need for accessory enzymes.
source: As opposed to other forms of regulation, such as phosphorylation, mechanoregulation is nearly instantaneous, and reversible without the need for accessory enzymes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an advantage of mechanoregulation.

claim: Examples of known catch bonds include cell adhesion through FimH, selectins, and vinculin.
source: Examples of known catch bonds range from cell adhesion through FimH (Thomas et al., 2002), selectins (Marshall et al., 2003), and vinculin (Huang et al., 2017), to outside-in signaling through integrins (Kong et al., 2009) and notch-jagged (Luca et al., 2017), to motor proteins including dynein (Kunwar et al., 2011) and myosin (Guo and Guilford, 2006), and even to kinetochore attachments during mitosis (Akiyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to studies on various catch bond systems.

claim: Examples of known catch bonds include outside-in signaling through integrins and notch-jagged.
source: Examples of known catch bonds range from cell adhesion through FimH (Thomas et al., 2002), selectins (Marshall et al., 2003), and vinculin (Huang et al., 2017), to outside-in signaling through integrins (Kong et al., 2009) and notch-jagged (Luca et al., 2017), to motor proteins including dynein (Kunwar et al., 2011) and myosin (Guo and Guilford, 2006), and even to kinetochore attachments during mitosis (Akiyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to studies on various catch bond systems.

claim: Examples of known catch bonds include motor proteins such as dynein and myosin.
source: Examples of known catch bonds range from cell adhesion through FimH (Thomas et al., 2002), selectins (Marshall et al., 2003), and vinculin (Huang et al., 2017), to outside-in signaling through integrins (Kong et al., 2009) and notch-jagged (Luca et al., 2017), to motor proteins including dynein (Kunwar et al., 2011) and myosin (Guo and Guilford, 2006), and even to kinetochore attachments during mitosis (Akiyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to studies on various catch bond systems.

claim: Examples of known catch bonds include kinetochore attachments during mitosis.
source: Examples of known catch bonds range from cell adhesion through FimH (Thomas et al., 2002), selectins (Marshall et al., 2003), and vinculin (Huang et al., 2017), to outside-in signaling through integrins (Kong et al., 2009) and notch-jagged (Luca et al., 2017), to motor proteins including dynein (Kunwar et al., 2011) and myosin (Guo and Guilford, 2006), and even to kinetochore attachments during mitosis (Akiyoshi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to studies on various catch bond systems.

claim: This work uncovers catch bonds between proteins involved in ribosome biogenesis.
source: Our data uncovers catch bonds between proteins involved in ribosome biogenesis, and, in contrast to these known examples, between a protein and more than one substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a novel finding of the study.

claim: This work demonstrates catch bonds between a protein and more than one substrate, in contrast to most known examples.
source: Our data uncovers catch bonds between proteins involved in ribosome biogenesis, and, in contrast to these known examples, between a protein and more than one substrate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a novel finding of the study.

claim: The MIDAS domain undocks from the AAA ring after the assembly factor dissociates from the pre-60S particle, relieving tension across the bond with the UBL domain.
source: Subsequently, the MIDAS domain undocks from the AAA ring, relieving tension across the bond with the UBL domain, deactivating the catch bond and facilitating assembly factor release.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed model for how catch bonds regulate the Mdn1 enzymatic cycle.

claim: Relieving tension deactivates the catch bond and facilitates assembly factor release.
source: Subsequently, the MIDAS domain undocks from the AAA ring, relieving tension across the bond with the UBL domain, deactivating the catch bond and facilitating assembly factor release.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as part of the proposed model for how catch bonds regulate the Mdn1 enzymatic cycle.

claim: The measured molecular weight of Rsa4-GFP by native mass spectrometry was 83.981 ± 0.001 kDa.
source: Expected mass (with loss of N-terminal methionine) 83.962 kDa (red dotted line), measured mass 83.981 ± 0.001 kDa (mean ± standard deviation, SD).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D caption.

claim: The expected mass of Rsa4-GFP (with loss of N-terminal methionine) is 83.962 kDa.
source: Expected mass (with loss of N-terminal methionine) 83.962 kDa (red dotted line), measured mass 83.981 ± 0.001 kDa (mean ± standard deviation, SD).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D caption.

claim: The similar values of the distance parameters xc and xs give rise to a roughly symmetric rise and fall in force-dependent bond lifetime, similar to the case of the P-selectin complex with sPSGL-1.
source: The similar values of the distance parameters xc and xs give rise to a roughly symmetric rise and fall in force-dependent bond lifetime, similar to the case of the P-selectin complex with sPSGL-1 (Barsegov and Thirumalai, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Barsegov and Thirumalai, 2005.

claim: Datasets generated with Rsa4-GFP and Rsa4-SNAP were in good agreement with each other, indicating that the GFP-GFP nanobody connection did not influence bond lifetime measurements.
source: Datasets generated with Rsa4-GFP and Rsa4-SNAP were in good agreement with each other (Figure 3—figure supplements 5–6), indicating that the GFP-GFP nanobody connection did not influence bond lifetime measurements.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to supplementary figures showing the comparison.

claim: All measured distributions of bond lifetimes could be fitted to a single exponential, indicating that applied force influenced the kinetics of dissociation, not the number of states from which dissociation could occur.
source: All measured distributions could be fitted to a single exponential (residuals and analysis in Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3), indicating that applied force influenced the kinetics of dissociation, not the number of states from which dissociation could occur (Huang et al., 2017).
